claims.text: The initial composite contains W particles or interconnected W ligaments embedded in a Cu matrix.
The initial W–Cu composite exhibits phase separation and interfacial voids.
A thin Ni interlayer should be deposited on W surfaces before consolidation.
Consolidation conditions must avoid excessive interdiffusion.
Combined high-heat-flux and irradiation exposure is representative of service at joints between W-based plasma-facing components and Cu-based cooling systems.
The Ni interlayer acts as a diffusion barrier.
The Ni interlayer enhances bonding at the W–Cu interface.
Ni reduces the chemical-potential difference between W and Cu.
The Ni interlayer improves wettability between W and Cu.
Improved W–Cu wettability and adhesion suppress interfacial void formation during thermal cycling and irradiation.
Improved W–Cu wettability and adhesion suppress phase separation during thermal cycling and irradiation.
Suppressing interfacial voids and phase separation stabilizes the composite microstructure.
A stabilized, less-voided interface facilitates superior thermal transport.
After matched heat-transfer and irradiation exposure, the Ni-interlayered composite will have fewer interfacial voids than the untreated composite.
After matched heat-transfer and irradiation exposure, the Ni-interlayered composite will exhibit less phase separation than the untreated composite.
The Ni-interlayered composite will have significantly higher thermal conductivity than the untreated composite under identical conditions.
Interfacial void formation and phase separation cause inferior thermal conductivity in untreated W–Cu composites.
The intervention is expected to be effective when the Ni interlayer is a few nanometers thick and thermal and irradiation fluxes are controlled.
The efficacy of the Ni interlayer may diminish at extreme temperatures or radiation doses.
An excessively thick Ni interlayer may introduce additional thermal resistance.
